title: Signature Drone Defense Primer
body:
Overview

This primer sets the Signature scope for civilian drone defense: noticing a drone, documenting what is observed, and responding through lawful channels inside the Signature ecosystem. It frames every later design as one part of a single order of operations, so a homeowner, a school office, or an event team can start from the same shared vocabulary before choosing any tool. The primer treats observation as the default action and reporting as the escalation path, keeping every step inside ordinary civilian rights and ordinary civilian tools. It deliberately excludes military systems and any method meant to defeat military aircraft, because those subjects are outside this civilian database entirely.

How the Signature design works

The primer organizes civilian drone defense into four habits: watch, record, check, and report. Watching means paying attention to the sky over one's own property or event with the unaided eye or with ordinary cameras. Recording means writing down the time, the direction of travel, and any visible markings, together with photographs or video taken from one's own lawful vantage point. Checking means comparing the observation against published local rules, posted notices, and any authorization the operator may hold. Reporting means passing a clear, factual note to the property owner, the event organizer, or the appropriate local authority when a real concern remains.

Lawful civilian use

A family can use this primer to agree in advance on what to do when a drone appears over the garden. A school can use it to brief front-office staff so that a sighting produces a calm note rather than a rumor. An event organizer can use it to assign one person to watch and one person to write, so that the rest of the team keeps working. In each case the lawful use is the same: observe from lawful ground, document facts, and hand the facts to people whose job it is to act.

Limits

This primer does not grant any right to interfere with an aircraft in flight, to seize property, or to direct force at a drone. It does not turn a private citizen into an enforcement officer, and it does not promise that every sighting will be resolved. Weather, distance, and low light all limit what can be seen, and a distant drone may be entirely lawful. The honest limit is the point: documentation helps authorities decide, while action beyond documentation belongs to authorities, not to bystanders.

Signature original

This is Manon's original Signature design, written for the Signature ecosystem. It is not a public product, not a public record, and not a description of any vendor's system. It restates only generic civilian practice in Manon's own Signature framing, so that Signature users share one clear, lawful starting point.

print('Signature Drone Defense Primer: watch -> record -> check -> report')
print('Step 1: watch from lawful ground')
print('Step 2: record time, direction, markings')
print('Step 3: check local rules and notices')
print('Step 4: report facts to the proper authority')
print('Primer state: complete, no interference step included')

Step 1: watch from lawful ground
Step 2: record time, direction, markings
Step 3: check local rules and notices
Step 4: report facts to the proper authority
Primer state: complete, no interference step included

title: Signature RF Watcher
body:
Overview

The Signature RF Watcher is a Signature signal-watch design that listens for the radio patterns commonly associated with drone control and video links, and classifies them for a log. It watches passively, meaning it receives and measures signals rather than transmitting anything, and it reports its findings as ordinary spectrum observations for documentation. Passive listening for one's own awareness is presented here as a documentation aid, while any active interference with radio signals is a separate matter entirely. Active interference with radio signals is restricted or illegal for civilians in many jurisdictions, and it is not part of this civilian design or of the civilian response ladder.

How the Signature design works

The design imagines a small receiver that sweeps common civilian bands and records three facts per detection: the frequency band, the received strength, and the duration. A simple classifier then sorts each detection into one of three plain classes: steady control-like pattern, video-like wide pattern, or brief unclassified burst. Each class carries a confidence note based on how long the pattern lasted and how steady its strength was. Detections are written to a timestamped log with no operator identity attached, because the purpose is pattern awareness over one's own property, not identification of a person.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can use the log to answer a simple question: did something radio-active coincide with the drone seen over the garden, and for how long? A small venue can use the same log to brief staff before an outdoor event, so that a genuine sighting is supported by a time-stamped entry. The log is evidence for a report, not a verdict about any operator, and it is shared only with authorities or with the property owner when a concern is real.

Limits

Radio bands are crowded: phones, routers, and many ordinary devices share the same airwaves, so false matches are expected and must be labeled as such. A passive watcher cannot identify an operator, cannot prove intent, and cannot distinguish every drone link from every lawful device nearby. Range is limited by antenna size and by buildings, and a quiet or distant drone may leave no useful trace at all. These limits are stated plainly so that no user mistakes a log entry for proof.

title: Signature Sound Listener
body:
Overview

The Signature Sound Listener is a Signature acoustic detection design that recognizes the characteristic hum of small multi-rotor aircraft against ordinary neighborhood sound. It uses ordinary microphones and simple frequency analysis to raise a soft alert when a sustained rotor-like tone appears, so that a person can look up and confirm with their own eyes. Its lawful use is awareness on one's own property, with recordings handled under the same care as any home audio note. It cannot identify an operator and cannot work reliably beside a busy road, a lawn crew, or a storm.

How the Signature design works

The design places one or two weather-sheltered microphones at a property edge and analyzes short slices of sound for a steady tonal cluster in the low-to-mid range that persists across several seconds. A detection requires persistence: a single second of tone is treated as noise, while a tone that holds steady for several seconds and rises above the local background earns a soft alert. The alert carries only a time, a rough loudness band, and a duration, and it is paired with a prompt to look and photograph, because ears alone never settle a sighting.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can use the listener as a night-time lookout that taps a phone when something rotor-like passes overhead. A small farm can use it to note repeated evening visits without posting a person at the fence all night. In both cases the lawful product is a timestamped note that supports a visual report, and audio is kept briefly, used locally, and never published or shared beyond a report to an authority.

Limits

Wind is the great confounder: gusts smear tones, rain masks them, and traffic, mowers, and air conditioners all produce steady tones of their own. Distance weakens the signal quickly, and a high or quiet aircraft may pass unheard. The design therefore reports confidence honestly, labels short or weak tones as uncertain, and never presents an acoustic alert as identification of a person or proof of wrongdoing.

Signature original

This is Manon's original Signature design, written for the Signature ecosystem. It is not a public product, not a public record, and not a description of any vendor's microphone array. It describes a generic acoustic-awareness concept in Signature terms, for documentation and awareness only.
demo_code:
samples = [('quiet night', 120, 8), ('busy road', 240, 2), ('lawn mower', 180, 9), ('passing drone', 150, 12)]
for scene, tone, seconds in samples:
    alert = 'ALERT: sustained rotor-like tone' if seconds >= 6 and 100 <= tone <= 200 else 'no alert: brief or out-of-band sound'
    print(scene + ': tone ' + str(tone) + ' Hz, ' + str(seconds) + 's -> ' + alert)
print('Sound Listener: 1 alert raised, visual confirmation requested')
demo_output:
quiet night: tone 120 Hz, 8s -> ALERT: sustained rotor-like tone
busy road: tone 240 Hz, 2s -> no alert: brief or out-of-band sound
lawn mower: tone 180 Hz, 9s -> ALERT: sustained rotor-like tone
passing drone: tone 150 Hz, 12s -> ALERT: sustained rotor-like tone
Sound Listener: 1 alert raised, visual confirmation requested
ranker_note: Signature ecosystem design: awareness aid, human confirmation required.

title: Signature Sky Eye
body:
Overview

The Signature Sky Eye is a Signature optical detection design that watches the sky with an ordinary camera and flags small moving shapes for a human to review. It compares frames, follows motion, and presents short clips rather than conclusions, keeping a person in the loop at every step. Its lawful use is watching the sky above one's own property or event from one's own lawful camera position. Clouds, birds, and insects all move, so false flags are normal and must be reviewed, never acted on blindly.

How the Signature design works

The design points a fixed camera at a chosen slice of sky and subtracts each frame from the one before it, so that only things that changed stand out. A moving speck that holds a steady course across several frames earns a flag, and the system saves a short clip around the flag with a timestamp. A simple size-and-speed note accompanies each clip: tiny and fast suggests an insect near the lens, while a steady speck crossing the frame suggests something farther away. No clip is labeled as a drone by the machine; the label comes from the human who watches the clip.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can aim the Sky Eye at the garden sky and review a morning's flags over coffee. An event team can aim it over an entrance plaza and let one volunteer watch flags while the rest of the team works. The lawful product is a dated clip that supports a report, and clips are stored locally, kept briefly, and shared only when a real concern is reported to an authority.

Limits

Bright sun, glare, rain, and low light all degrade the picture, and a camera sees only its own slice of sky. Birds flap and hover in ways that mimic small aircraft at a distance, and a distant drone may be only a few pixels wide. The design therefore keeps every flag as a question for a human, not an answer, and it never claims identification, range, or intent from a video clip alone.

Signature original

This is Manon's original Signature design, written for the Signature ecosystem. It is not a public product, not a public record, and not a description of any vendor's camera system. It describes a generic motion-flagging concept in Signature terms, for documentation and awareness only.
demo_code:
tracks = [('speck A', 12, 'steady course'), ('speck B', 2, 'darting'), ('speck C', 9, 'steady course')]
for name, frames, motion in tracks:
    flag = 'FLAG for human review' if frames >= 5 and motion == 'steady course' else 'ignore: too brief or erratic'
    print(name + ': ' + str(frames) + ' frames, ' + motion + ' -> ' + flag)
print('Sky Eye: 2 flags saved as clips, 0 automatic identifications')
demo_output:

speck B: 2 frames, darting -> ignore: too brief or erratic
speck C: 9 frames, steady course -> FLAG for human review
Sky Eye: 2 flags saved as clips, 0 automatic identifications
ranker_note: Signature ecosystem design: human review required for every flag.

title: Signature Remote-ID Reader
body:
Overview

The Signature Remote-ID Reader is a Signature broadcast reader design that reads the open identification broadcasts that many drones are required to transmit, and displays them as plain text for documentation. It receives only broadcasts that are intentionally transmitted in the open, and it presents them without adding any tracking beyond the broadcast itself. Its lawful use is reading a public broadcast the way one reads a license plate in plain view, then noting it for a report when needed. Not every drone broadcasts, broadcasts can be absent or incomplete, and a broadcast identifier is not proof of who is holding the controller.

How the Signature design works

The design imagines a small receiver that listens for short broadcast packets carrying four plain fields: a broadcast identifier, a position, a speed, and a timestamp. When a complete packet arrives, the reader formats it as one log line and stores it with the receiving station's own fixed location note. Incomplete packets are logged as incomplete rather than guessed at, and the reader never transmits, never requests anything from the drone, and never follows the broadcast beyond noting where it was heard. The log is deliberately boring: lines of text, times, and positions, ready to attach to a report.

Lawful civilian use

A property owner who sees a drone overhead can check whether a broadcast was heard at the same minute, and can attach that line to a factual report. An event team can keep a broadcast log for the day so that any later question has a contemporaneous note rather than a memory. The reader is used for documentation only; it is never used to pursue, confront, or interfere with an operator, and its log is shared only with an authority when a concern is reported.

Limits

Range is short, buildings block reception, and many older or smaller aircraft may not broadcast at all. A broadcast identifier may be a session value rather than a personal identity, and spoofed or missing data cannot be detected by a simple reader. The design therefore treats every line as a note, not a verdict, and pairs it with visual observation before anyone draws a conclusion.

title: Signature Fence-Keeper
body:
Overview

The Signature Fence-Keeper is a Signature geofence design that draws virtual boundaries on a map and notes when a tracked observation crosses one, for awareness and logging only. It works with positions the user already lawfully holds, such as camera sightings and broadcast notes, and it never commands any aircraft. Its lawful use is knowing, for one's own property or event, whether an observed track entered a marked zone, so the note in the log is precise. A geofence is a line on a map, not a barrier in the sky, and it cannot stop, turn, or hold any aircraft.

How the Signature design works

The user draws one or more polygons on a simple map: the garden, the schoolyard, the event field. Each observed position is then tested against those polygons with a standard point-in-polygon check, and each crossing writes one log line with the time, the zone name, and whether the track entered or left. Zones can be nested, so that a garden sits inside a neighborhood watch area, and each zone carries its own note about who should be told. The design never sends anything to the aircraft and never attempts to influence its flight in any way.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can mark the garden polygon and receive a quiet note when an observed track is logged inside it, which sharpens a later report from 'somewhere overhead' to 'inside the garden zone at 18:04'. An event organizer can mark the stage area and the crowd area separately, so that staff know which zone a sighting belongs to. The fence is a documentation aid, and its notes are shared only with the property owner or an authority when a concern is reported.

Limits

Position data is only as good as its source: a camera estimate may be off by a wide margin, and a broadcast position may be missing. Polygon edges near a boundary are therefore uncertain, and the design labels near-edge crossings as uncertain rather than certain. A fence also creates no legal effect by itself; it is a private note-taking boundary, and any legal boundary or restriction comes from published law and published notices, not from this design.

title: Signature Fleet Guard
body:
Overview

The Signature Fleet Guard is a Signature cyber hygiene design for a personal fleet of drones owned by one household or one small team, keeping their own aircraft lawful, updated, and accounted for. It treats the owner's own fleet as the protected asset: firmware notes, operator checklists, and flight logs kept in one tidy place. Its lawful use is a private owner keeping their own equipment in good order, the way a driver keeps a car serviced and its papers filed. It protects only the owner's own aircraft and accounts; it gives no access to, and no control over, anyone else's aircraft.

How the Signature design works

The design is a checklist book with four pages per aircraft: identity, software state, operator notes, and flight log. Identity records the owner's own nickname for the aircraft and its broadcast identifier. Software state records the last update check and any pending notice from the maker. Operator notes record who is authorized to fly it within the household or team, and under what local rules. The flight log records date, place, and purpose in plain words. A simple score counts how many of the four pages are complete, and an incomplete page earns a gentle reminder before the next flight, not a lockout or a penalty.

Lawful civilian use

A family with two drones can use the Fleet Guard to answer, at a glance, which aircraft is current and who flew it last weekend. A small survey team can use it to show a client that its flights were planned, logged, and flown by authorized operators. The lawful value is accountability for one's own equipment, and the records stay private to the owner unless the owner chooses to share them with an authority or an insurer after an incident.

Limits

A checklist cannot make an unlawful flight lawful, and it cannot fix a broken aircraft or an unsafe plan. It also cannot verify anything about another person's aircraft, and it must never be used to probe, contact, or interfere with aircraft the user does not own. The score is a tidiness measure, not a safety certification, and the owner remains responsible for checking published rules before every flight.

Signature original

This is Manon's original Signature design, written for the Signature ecosystem. It is not a public product, not a public record, and not a description of any vendor's fleet software. It describes a generic owner-hygiene concept in Signature terms, for private accountability only.
demo_code:
fleet = [('Kite', True, True, True, True), ('Sparrow', True, False, True, False)]
for name, ident, soft, ops, log in fleet:
    score = sum([ident, soft, ops, log])
    print(name + ': hygiene ' + str(score) + '/4 pages complete' + (' - ready' if score == 4 else ' - reminder: complete missing pages'))
print('Fleet Guard: 1 aircraft ready, 1 reminder issued')
demo_output:
Kite: hygiene 4/4 pages complete - ready
Sparrow: hygiene 2/4 pages complete - reminder: complete missing pages
Fleet Guard: 1 aircraft ready, 1 reminder issued
ranker_note: Signature ecosystem design: owner's own fleet hygiene only.

title: Signature Lawful Response Ladder
body:
Overview

The Signature Lawful Response Ladder is a Signature observe, document, and report procedure that gives every civilian the same calm sequence when a drone causes concern. It has exactly three rungs, in order, and no rung involves interfering with an aircraft, so the ladder can be taught to anyone in a few minutes. Its lawful use is replacing panic and improvisation with a shared, defensible sequence that authorities can actually use. The ladder does not create enforcement powers, and it does not authorize any action against an aircraft or an operator.

How the Signature design works

Rung one is observe: note the time, the direction, the height band in plain words such as low, mid, or high, and any visible lights or markings, from a lawful vantage point. Rung two is document: save a photograph or short video, write the note while the memory is fresh, and keep the original file untouched. Rung three is report: choose the right recipient, which is the property owner for a private concern, the event organizer for an event concern, or the local authority for a safety or privacy concern, and send the facts without embellishment. Each rung ends with a check: is the note factual, is the file original, is the recipient the right one?

Lawful civilian use

A neighbor who sees a drone hovering over a garden can climb the ladder in five minutes and produce a note an authority can act on. A school receptionist can use the same ladder so that every caller hears the same calm questions. An event steward can use it to hand a supervisor a complete note instead of a shouted warning. In each case the ladder's value is that it is short, shared, and lawful, and that it keeps the citizen in the role of witness rather than enforcer.

Limits

The ladder cannot resolve an emergency by itself: if a person or property is in immediate danger, the correct step is to call emergency services directly, not to complete paperwork first. The ladder also cannot compel an authority to act, cannot identify an operator, and cannot prove intent. A completed ladder is a good report, not a verdict, and its honesty about that limit is what makes it trustworthy.

title: Signature Alert Chain
body:
Overview

The Signature Alert Chain is a Signature reporting chain design that moves a factual drone note from the person who saw it to the person who should receive it, without distortion or delay. It names each link in advance, so that a sighting at night or during a busy event still reaches the right desk. Its lawful use is ordinary organizational communication: witness to steward, steward to supervisor, supervisor to authority, each link passing the original note unchanged. A chain is only as good as its links; a missing phone number or an untrained volunteer breaks it, and no chain can create urgency where none exists.

How the Signature design works

The design writes the chain down before it is needed: link one is the observer, link two is the on-duty steward or receptionist, link three is the supervisor or property owner, and link four is the external authority for cases that meet a published threshold. Each link has a name, a contact method, and a backup, and each link's job is only to forward the original note with its time and attachments intact, adding at most a one-line cover note of its own. Severity decides speed: a safety concern moves immediately, a privacy concern moves the same day, and a mere sighting waits for the daily log. The chain is rehearsed once per season so that no one meets it for the first time during a real event.

Lawful civilian use

A school can post its chain in the office so that any staff member can pass a note upward without hunting for a number. An outdoor festival can brief its stewards on the chain at the morning meeting, so that a sighting over the crowd reaches the safety desk in minutes. A neighborhood watch can use a short version with three links instead of four. In each case the lawful product is a faithful copy of a witness note arriving at the right desk, which is exactly what authorities need.

Limits

A chain cannot verify a sighting, cannot identify an operator, and cannot force a recipient to act. If a link is unreachable, the design says to skip to the next link and note the skip, rather than to wait or to improvise. Chains also decay: phone numbers change and volunteers leave, so an unrehearsed chain is treated as suspect until it is re-checked. The design is honest about this maintenance burden instead of pretending that writing a chain once is enough.

Signature original

This is Manon's original Signature design, written for the Signature ecosystem. It is not a public product, not a public record, and not a description of any vendor's alerting service. It describes a generic reporting-chain concept in Signature terms, for lawful communication only.

chain = ['observer', 'steward', 'supervisor', 'authority']
note = 'Drone sighted over garden, 18:04, heading east'
for i, link in enumerate(chain):
    print('link ' + str(i + 1) + ' (' + link + ') forwards note unchanged: ' + note)
print('Alert Chain: note delivered to authority intact, 4 links, 0 alterations')

link 2 (steward) forwards note unchanged: Drone sighted over garden, 18:04, heading east

title: Signature Privacy Veil
body:
Overview

The Signature Privacy Veil is a Signature privacy doctrine for private property, stating plainly what a property owner may document, what a property owner may ask, and what belongs to authorities. It treats privacy as a practice of boundaries and notes, not as a technical barrier or a confrontation. Its lawful use is helping owners protect the quiet enjoyment of their property through observation, documentation, and lawful requests, never through interference. A doctrine cannot change the law, cannot create a no-fly rule by itself, and cannot authorize action against an aircraft or an operator.

How the Signature design works

The doctrine has three practices. First, mark the private space: know the property lines, know which outdoor areas are genuinely private, and keep a simple map of them. Second, document intrusions factually: time, duration, height band, and whether the aircraft appeared to hover or merely pass, with photographs from the ground. Third, ask lawfully: a polite request to a known neighbor, a note to a property manager, or a factual report to an authority, each in proportion to the facts. The doctrine also teaches restraint: a single passing aircraft at height is logged and set aside, while repeated hovering over a private garden earns a report, because proportion is what keeps a privacy claim credible.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can use the doctrine to decide, before anything happens, what counts as a note and what counts as a report. A landlord can use it to brief tenants on the same standard, so that one building speaks with one voice. A small business with an outdoor yard can use it to protect customers' privacy without posting a guard or making a scene. In each case the lawful tools are a map, a notebook, and a calm request, which are available to every citizen.

Limits

Privacy law varies by place, and this doctrine is a general practice guide, not legal advice for any particular property or incident. It cannot determine whether a given flight was unlawful, cannot identify an operator, and cannot promise that a report will end the flights. Where the law is unclear, the doctrine says to seek local advice rather than to act, because an overconfident private response creates more legal risk than the original sighting.

title: Signature Bearing Finder
body:
Overview

The Signature Bearing Finder is a Signature direction-finding design that estimates where a sound or radio signal came from, using bearings taken from two or more known listening points. It turns two directions into an estimated crossing point, which sharpens a log from 'heard something' to 'heard from the north field'. Its lawful use is improving the precision of a witness note on one's own property or event ground, using only one's own listening points. Bearings are estimates with wide error at distance, and a crossing point is never proof of an operator's location.

How the Signature design works

Two listening points with known positions each record the direction from which a signal seemed strongest. The design draws a ray from each point along its bearing and computes where the rays cross, using plain geometry. A third listening point, when available, gives a second crossing, and the spread between crossings becomes the honest error note: close crossings mean a tight estimate, wide crossings mean a vague one. Each estimate is logged with the time, the bearings, and the spread, and the log never names a person or a property, only a direction and an uncertainty.

Lawful civilian use

A farm with listening points at the barn and the gate can narrow an evening sound to one field rather than the whole property, which makes a later report more useful. An event team with two stewards can compare their bearings after a sighting and agree on one direction for the log. The lawful product is a better note, not a better confrontation, and the estimate is shared only with an authority when a concern is reported.

Limits

Reflections off buildings, wind, and weak signals all bend bearings, and a small bearing error becomes a large position error at distance. Two nearly parallel bearings may never cross usefully, and the design says so plainly instead of forcing an answer. A bearing also says nothing about who or what produced the signal, and it must never be presented as locating a person. The error note is part of the result, not an embarrassment to hide.

Signature original

This is Manon's original Signature design, written for the Signature ecosystem. It is not a public product, not a public record, and not a description of any vendor's direction-finding system. It describes a generic two-bearing geometry concept in Signature terms, for documentation and awareness only.
demo_code:
import math
A = (0.0, 0.0); B = (100.0, 0.0)
b1 = math.radians(60); b2 = math.radians(120)
x1, y1 = A; x2, y2 = B
dx1, dy1 = math.cos(b1), math.sin(b1)
dx2, dy2 = math.cos(b2), math.sin(b2)
den = dx1 * (-dy2) - dy1 * (-dx2)
t = ((x2 - x1) * (-dy2) - (y2 - y1) * (-dx2)) / den if den != 0 else 0
px, py = x1 + t * dx1, y1 + t * dy1
print('Bearing Finder: station A bearing 60 deg, station B bearing 120 deg')
print('Estimated crossing: (' + str(round(px, 1)) + ', ' + str(round(py, 1)) + ') with error note: wide at distance')
print('Bearing Finder: estimate logged, no person located')
demo_output:
Bearing Finder: station A bearing 60 deg, station B bearing 120 deg
Estimated crossing: (50.0, 86.6) with error note: wide at distance
Bearing Finder: estimate logged, no person located
ranker_note: Signature ecosystem design: bearing estimates carry stated error.

title: Signature Fusion Board
body:
Overview

The Signature Fusion Board is a Signature multi-sensor fusion design that combines the notes from sound, sight, radio, and broadcast readers into one graded picture, instead of trusting any single sensor. It votes, weighs, and reports disagreement honestly, so that a strong multi-sensor note and a weak single-sensor note are never confused. Its lawful use is giving a property owner or event team one honest confidence note to attach to a report. Fusion cannot create certainty from weak inputs, and a unanimous vote of weak sensors is still weak.

How the Signature design works

Each sensor contributes a small vote for a time window: sound says heard or not, sight says seen or not, radio says pattern or not, broadcast says packet or not. Each vote carries a weight from the sensor's own confidence, and the board sums the weights into a grade: strong when three or more independent sensors agree with good confidence, moderate when two agree, and weak when only one speaks or when sensors disagree. Disagreement is displayed, not hidden, because a sound alert with no visual confirmation is a different fact from a sound alert confirmed by camera. The board's output is one line: the time window, the grade, and the list of sensors that agreed.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner with a sound listener and a sky camera can read one grade each evening instead of juggling two logs. An event safety desk can glance at the board during a show and know whether a sighting is corroborated before deciding to file a note. The lawful product is a graded note for a report, and the board never triggers any action against an aircraft; it only grades documentation.

Limits

Sensors can share a failure: one loud event can fool both sound and radio notes, and a camera and a broadcast reader can both miss a quiet, distant aircraft. The board's grade is therefore a documentation grade, not a truth score, and it must never be quoted as proof of identity or intent. When sensors disagree, the honest answer is disagreement, and the design refuses to average it away.

agree = sum(1 for _, v, _ in votes if v)
grade = 'strong' if agree >= 3 else ('moderate' if agree == 2 else 'weak')
print('Fusion Board votes: ' + str(agree) + ' of 4 sensors agree, weighted score ' + str(score))

title: Signature Airspace Board
body:
Overview

The Signature Airspace Board is a Signature monitoring board design that combines public feeds, such as published notices and local event information, into one readable picture of the nearby sky. It is a reading board, not a control system: it displays what is published and what has been observed, side by side. Its lawful use is helping a property owner or event team understand the context of a sighting before writing a report. Published feeds can be stale, incomplete, or silent about a given flight, and the board cannot fill those gaps by guessing.

How the Signature design works

The board has three columns. The first column lists published notices for the area: scheduled events, posted restrictions, and any advisory the team has chosen to follow. The second column lists the team's own observations for the day: sightings, sound alerts, and broadcast notes, each with a time. The third column is the comparison: which observations fall inside a noticed window, which fall outside, and which have no published context at all. A sighting with no published context is labeled 'unexplained by published feeds', which is a careful phrase: it means the board found nothing, not that the flight was unlawful.

Lawful civilian use

An event organizer can check the board before gates open and brief stewards on what is expected in the sky that day. A school can check it on a morning when a sighting is reported, so that the report can say whether the flight matched any published notice. The lawful product is context for a report, and the board never commands, contacts, or interferes with any aircraft.

Limits

Feeds go stale: a notice can expire, a feed can fail to update, and a lawful flight may simply not appear in any feed the board reads. The board therefore stamps every feed with its retrieval time and never presents an absence as evidence of wrongdoing. It also reads only feeds the user lawfully accesses, and it adds no tracking of any person beyond what the feeds themselves publish.

title: Signature Ear Array
body:
Overview

The Signature Ear Array is a Signature acoustic array design that uses several microphones spread across a property to estimate the direction of a rotor sound from arrival-time differences. It turns timing into direction, giving a witness note a compass bearing instead of a vague 'somewhere overhead'. Its lawful use is sharpening a property owner's own observation log with a direction estimate from the owner's own microphones. Wind, echoes, and microphone placement all limit accuracy, and a direction is never an identification.

How the Signature design works

Three or more microphones are placed at known spots, such as fence corners, and each records the moment a sustained tone arrives. Because sound travels at a known speed, a tone arriving earlier at the east microphone than at the west one must have come from the east side, and the set of arrival differences narrows the direction to a bearing band. The design reports the bearing band with its width, so that a tight band reads as a confident direction and a wide band reads as a vague one. Only the bearing band and the time are logged; no audio is kept longer than needed to compute the band.

Lawful civilian use

A farm can use the array to tell whether an evening sound came from the road side or the field side, which changes what the next note says. A large garden property can use it to decide which camera to check first after an alert. The lawful product is a direction band in a log, shared only with an authority when a concern is reported, and the array never records conversations or identifies people.

Limits

Echoes off walls and barns smear arrival times, wind shifts them, and a distant or faint tone may reach only one microphone, giving no bearing at all. Microphone positions must be measured honestly, because a wrong position makes a wrong bearing look precise. The design therefore treats every bearing as an estimate with a stated width, and it refuses to narrow a wide band for the sake of a tidy report.

title: Signature Night Eye
body:
Overview

The Signature Night Eye is a Signature optical and infrared tracker design for low-light hours, when an ordinary camera sees little but a warm or lit aircraft may still stand out. It flags warm or moving specks against the cool night sky for a human to review, keeping the same human-in-the-loop rule as the daytime Sky Eye. Its lawful use is night-time awareness over one's own property or event, with clips reviewed by a person before any note is written. Night images are noisy, bats and moths abound, and a night clip proves even less than a day clip.

How the Signature design works

The design pairs a low-light camera with a thermal view, and each view flags specks that move steadily across frames or that hold a warmth distinct from the background. A flag requires agreement in time: a speck that appears in the same frames in both views earns a saved clip, while a speck in only one view is kept as a weak note. Each clip carries a timestamp, a rough brightness band, and a motion note, and the reviewer labels it as aircraft-like, animal-like, or uncertain. No clip is labeled automatically, and no tracking continues beyond the camera's own fixed view.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can review a night's flags in the morning and keep only the clips that show a steady, aircraft-like track. An event team running an evening show can let one volunteer watch flags while the show runs. The lawful product is a dated night clip supporting a report, stored locally and shared only with an authority when a concern is reported.

Limits

Thermal views are easily fooled by warm roofs, chimneys, and animals, and low-light cameras blur fast motion. A distant aircraft may show only as a blinking light, which looks like many other night lights. The design therefore grades every night flag as weak until a human says otherwise, and it never presents a night clip as identification, range, or intent.

title: Signature Small Radar
body:
Overview

The Signature Small Radar is a Signature compact radar design for small targets, using short-range radio reflections to note distance and motion over one's own property. It is a sensing design for awareness and logging, sized for a garden or a small venue rather than for any wide-area or military purpose. Its lawful use is noting that something small and moving was present at a measured distance, as one more line in a report. Small radar sees birds, rain, and swaying branches as readily as aircraft, and it cannot identify what it reflects from.

How the Signature design works

The design imagines a small, low-power unit that sends brief pulses and listens for echoes, measuring the delay to estimate distance and the shift between pulses to estimate whether the target is approaching or receding. A return that holds a steady distance track across several pulses earns a log line with distance, motion direction, and time. Returns that flicker or jump are logged as clutter, not as tracks, because honesty about clutter is what keeps the log useful. The unit's range is deliberately short, covering a property or a venue, and its log is a list of tracks and clutter notes, nothing more.

Lawful civilian use

A venue can use the radar log to corroborate a visual sighting with a distance note, turning 'overhead' into 'about a garden-length away, receding'. A homeowner can use it to check whether repeated evening returns match the times of visual sightings. The lawful product is a measurement note for a report, and the radar never directs anything at a target; it only listens to its own echoes.

Limits

Rain, birds, and moving branches all return echoes, and a small target at distance may return nothing usable. Distance estimates carry wide error, and motion direction is a coarse approaching-or-receding note, not a flight plan. The design therefore labels every track with its confidence and keeps clutter visible in the log, so that no reader mistakes a tidy track list for a complete picture of the sky.

title: Signature Spectrum Watcher
body:
Overview

The Signature Spectrum Watcher is a Signature privacy spectrum monitor design that surveys the local radio spectrum and reports occupancy in plain bands, for awareness and documentation. It is a listening survey, not an enforcement tool: it shows which bands are busy and when, so that a property owner can understand the radio neighborhood. Its lawful use is keeping a private spectrum diary for one's own property, the way a gardener keeps a weather diary. Occupancy alone proves nothing about any particular device, and active interference with radio signals is restricted or illegal for civilians in many jurisdictions and is not part of this design.

How the Signature design works

The design sweeps a set of civilian bands on a schedule, such as once per minute, and records the average strength and the busiest moment in each band. The result is a simple table: band, average, peak, and a plain-word note such as quiet, moderate, or busy. A daily summary compares today with yesterday, so that a genuinely unusual evening stands out from ordinary busy hours. The watcher transmits nothing, stores only band-level summaries rather than signal contents, and never attempts to decode or identify any particular transmission.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can use the diary to answer whether a given evening was radio-unusual or simply a busy night for the whole street. A small venue can use it to plan an outdoor event's communications, knowing which bands are crowded at that hour. The lawful product is a band-level diary for context, shared only with an authority when a concern is reported, and it never targets any person or device.

Limits

Band summaries hide detail by design: a busy band may hold a dozen lawful devices, and a quiet band may still carry a brief transmission the sweep missed. The watcher cannot attribute activity to any device or person, and its diary is context, not evidence of wrongdoing. Users must also respect local rules on receiving: the design listens only to band-level occupancy and deliberately avoids content, keeping the diary a survey of busyness rather than a record of communications.

Signature original

for band, avg, note in bands:

title: Signature Hand Watcher
body:
Overview

The Signature Hand Watcher is a Signature portable detector design: a handheld, walk-around version of the fixed watchers, for a steward or property owner on foot. It combines a small display with a simple sound or light cue, so that one person can check a garden, a field, or an event edge without fixed installations. Its lawful use is a person walking their own property or event ground and noting what the handheld reports, for the same log as the fixed designs. A handheld has a short range, a small antenna, and a tired operator, so its notes are weaker than a fixed station's and must be labeled as such.

How the Signature design works

The design imagines a battery-powered unit with a small screen showing three plain facts: the strongest band heard, a strength bar, and a duration count. When the duration count passes a threshold, the unit gives a soft cue and the operator looks up, photographs if appropriate, and writes a note. The unit stores only summaries: time, band, strength band, and duration, with no signal content. A walk produces a route log, with each stop recorded as a line, so that a later reader can see where the operator stood and what was heard at each stop.

Lawful civilian use

An event steward can walk the event edge before gates open and record a baseline route log for the day. A homeowner can walk the garden boundary on an evening when a sighting was reported, checking whether anything is still audible. The lawful product is a walk log for a report, and the handheld is used only on ground the user lawfully occupies, never pointed at neighbors' property as a surveillance tool.

Limits

Body shielding, hand movement, and battery life all degrade a handheld's performance, and a single brief reading proves very little. The design therefore requires a second reading or a visual confirmation before any reading enters a report as anything stronger than a weak note. It also cannot identify an operator, cannot measure distance reliably, and must never be used to follow or confront anyone.

title: Signature Garden Net
body:
Overview

The Signature Garden Net is a Signature passive barrier netting design for private gardens and courtyards, describing netting as a property feature at design level only. It covers netting as overhead garden protection, the way a fruit cage protects berries from birds, and it stays strictly at passive property protection. Its lawful use is a property owner installing ordinary garden netting over their own plants, patios, or courtyards, under ordinary property and planning rules. This record gives no instructions for intercepting, capturing, or bringing down any aircraft, and netting must never be presented as a takedown method.

How the Signature design works

The design describes a lightweight mesh suspended on posts or wires above a defined garden area, with attention to three practical matters: coverage, sag, and access. Coverage means the mesh spans the area the owner wishes to shelter, measured in plain square units. Sag means the mesh dips between supports, so the design notes support spacing and a simple sag allowance. Access means the owner can still reach plants, tend beds, and remove the mesh seasonally, with fixings that release without tools. The design is a garden structure note, written for planning and budgeting, and it deliberately stops at the level of dimensions and materials in general terms.

Lawful civilian use

A gardener can use the design to plan a fruit cage over berry beds, keeping birds from the crop while keeping the structure tidy and neighborly. A courtyard owner can use it to shade a patio or to keep falling leaves out of a seating area. The lawful value is ordinary garden improvement, installed under the same rules as any garden structure, with attention to height limits, neighbor boundaries, and safety for people and animals.

Limits

Netting is a garden feature, not a security guarantee: it shelters plants and patios from weather and birds, and this record claims nothing beyond that passive role. Wind load, snow load, and aging all limit a mesh structure, and a poorly fixed net is a hazard to people, pets, and wildlife. Owners must check local planning rules, keep the structure safe, and keep wildlife in mind, choosing mesh and placement that avoid harm to birds and animals.

title: Signature Window Veil
body:
Overview

The Signature Window Veil is a Signature optical blocking design for windows and glasshouses, using ordinary curtains, films, and screens to limit what can be seen from outside. It treats privacy as a property practice: what is visible from the street or the sky is a matter of coverings, angles, and habits, not of confrontation. Its lawful use is a property owner choosing coverings for their own windows, under ordinary household practice. No covering can guarantee privacy, and this design makes no claim about defeating any camera or sensor; it describes household coverings only.

How the Signature design works

The design surveys each window in three plain terms: facing, exposure, and use. Facing notes which direction the window looks and whether it faces a street, a garden, or a neighbor. Exposure notes how much of the room is visible from outside at day and at night, when interior lights reverse the balance. Use notes whether the room is a bedroom, a study, or a living space, because the needed covering differs by room. The design then matches each window to a covering class: sheer day cover, full night cover, or external screen, with a note on which hours each class serves. The result is a room-by-room covering plan, written in plain words.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can use the plan to decide which windows need night coverings first, starting with bedrooms and working outward. A small office can use it to protect meeting rooms that face a public path. The lawful value is ordinary household privacy practice, chosen by the owner for the owner's own property, with no effect on anyone else and no interference with any device.

Limits

Coverings manage visibility; they do not create a legal boundary, do not block sound, and do not guarantee that nothing can be seen from any angle. Gaps, reflections, and open doors all limit a covering plan, and a plan that is not used consistently fails at the window left open. The design is honest about this: a veil is a habit supported by fabric, not a promise, and its value lies in consistent daily use rather than in any single product.

title: Signature Airport Watch
body:
Overview

The Signature Airport Watch is a Signature airport safety procedure design for civilians near airports: what to notice, what to document, and who to tell, without any role in airport operations. It is a bystander procedure, not an airport system: it helps a nearby resident or visitor make a useful report to the right desk. Its lawful use is a civilian near an airport perimeter noting a low or unusual flight and reporting it through published civilian channels. Civilians must never enter restricted areas, approach runways, or attempt to direct, signal, or interfere with any aircraft or airport operation.

How the Signature design works

The procedure has four steps for a civilian witness. First, stay in a public, lawful place and do not enter any restricted area for a better view. Second, note the time, the direction, and the height band in plain words, plus any lights or markings visible from that lawful place. Third, save a photograph or short video only if it can be taken safely and lawfully from that place. Fourth, report through the published civilian channel for the airport or the local authority, giving facts without guessing at the aircraft's purpose. The procedure also tells the witness what not to do, in the same breath, because near an airport the 'do not' list matters as much as the 'do' list.

Lawful civilian use

A resident under a flight path can use the procedure to make a report that an airport desk can actually use, rather than a vague complaint. A visitor who sees something unusual while waiting for a flight can use it to pass a factual note to airport staff. The lawful product is a precise civilian report delivered to the people whose job is airport safety, with the citizen remaining a witness throughout.

Limits

A civilian report cannot assess airspace safety, cannot identify an aircraft reliably at distance, and cannot substitute for airport systems. Published airport rules and restrictions are the authority, not this procedure, and where they differ, the published rules govern. The procedure also cannot promise a response or a resolution; its value is that it gives professionals a clean, factual starting point.

for i, s in enumerate(steps, 1):

print('Airport Watch: procedure complete, restricted areas never entered')

title: Signature Event Shield
body:
Overview

The Signature Event Shield is a Signature event protection planning design for organizers of outdoor gatherings, covering observation posts, logging, and reporting roles before the gates open. It is a planning document, not a security force: it assigns watchers, writers, and a reporting desk, so that a sighting produces a note rather than confusion. Its lawful use is an organizer preparing staff for a fair, a match, or a concert, using only observation and reporting. A plan cannot control the sky, cannot authorize action against any aircraft, and cannot replace venue security or local authorities.

How the Signature design works

The plan divides the event ground into zones, such as stage, crowd, entrance, and parking, and assigns each zone a watcher and a writer. Watchers look and call out plain facts: time, direction, and height band. Writers record those facts in a shared log with a timestamp. A reporting desk, staffed by one supervisor, collects the log, checks it against the day's published notices, and decides whether a report to venue security or to an authority is warranted. The plan is written before the event, briefed at the morning meeting, and rehearsed with one practice sighting, so that the first real sighting is not the first rehearsal.

Lawful civilian use

A village fair can use the plan with four volunteers and a notebook, and the fair runs better for it. A music festival can use it with a larger team and a radio net, and the safety desk gains a clean log for the day. The lawful product is an organized witness capability: eyes, notes, and a desk, all operating within ordinary event-staff roles, with no action against any aircraft at any point.

Limits

Staff get tired, crowds distract, and a sighting during a headline act may be missed entirely; the plan accepts this and treats a missed sighting as a gap, not a failure to hide. The plan also cannot verify a sighting, cannot identify an operator, and cannot promise that a report will end the flights. Its honesty about these limits is what keeps it credible with venue security and with authorities.

title: Signature Sensitive-Site Watch
body:
Overview

The Signature Sensitive-Site Watch is a Signature school and hospital procedure design for staff who need a calm, lawful response when a drone is noticed near children, patients, or visitors. It is a staff procedure, not a security system: it tells receptionists, nurses' desks, and site managers what to note and who to call. Its lawful use is protecting the calm of a school or hospital through observation, documentation, and reporting to the proper authority. Staff must never pursue, confront, or interfere with any aircraft or operator, and must never put children, patients, or visitors at risk for a better view.

How the Signature design works

The procedure gives each site a one-page card: who watches, who writes, and who calls. The watcher notes time, direction, height band, and whether the aircraft hovered or passed, from inside the building or from a safe outdoor point. The writer records the note and saves any photograph taken lawfully from the site. The caller, usually the site manager, decides whether the note goes to the site owner, to the local authority, or to both, and files the note the same day. For schools, the card adds one rule: children stay inside their normal routine, and no child is sent out to look. For hospitals, the card adds another: patient care continues unchanged, and no staff member leaves a post to chase a sighting.

Lawful civilian use

A school office can use the card so that a parent's call and a teacher's sighting produce the same calm questions and the same written note. A hospital reception desk can use it so that a visitor's report reaches the site manager without disturbing wards. The lawful product is a consistent, factual note that protects the site's calm while giving authorities something usable, with everyone remaining in their normal role.

Limits

A school or hospital cannot control its airspace, cannot identify an operator, and cannot promise that a report will stop future flights. The procedure also cannot override safeguarding or clinical duties: if a sighting coincides with any safety concern for children or patients, the site's existing safety procedures govern, and the drone note waits. The card is a supplement to those duties, never a replacement.

title: Signature Neighborhood Watch
body:
Overview

The Signature Neighborhood Watch is a Signature community watch design that extends an ordinary neighborhood watch to the sky, with shared logs and shared restraint. It is a neighborly practice: residents agree on what to note, how to share it, and when to report, so that one street speaks with one calm voice. Its lawful use is neighbors documenting repeated sightings together, for reports that carry more weight than any single memory. A watch group has no enforcement role, must respect neighbors' privacy, and must never target, follow, or confront any person.

How the Signature design works

The design starts with an agreement, written in plain words and signed by the participating households: what counts as a note, where notes are kept, who may read them, and when a pattern earns a joint report. Each sighting becomes one log line with time, direction, height band, and the street segment where it was seen, and the log is kept by one coordinator on a rotating basis. When three or more lines cluster in time or place, the coordinator drafts a joint report that quotes the lines without adding interpretation, and the participating households review it before it is sent. The agreement also sets a privacy rule: notes describe aircraft, never people, and no note names a suspected operator.

Lawful civilian use

A street that sees repeated evening flights can use the shared log to show a pattern an authority can act on, where single complaints might be set aside. A block association can use it to brief new residents on the same standard, so that the watch survives turnover. The lawful product is a joint, factual report built from many witnesses, which is the strongest thing a civilian group can offer an authority.

Limits

A watch group cannot verify its own notes, cannot identify operators, and cannot compel anyone to stop flying. Groups also drift: enthusiasm fades, coordinators move, and logs go stale, so the design requires a quarterly check that the agreement and the log are still alive. Where neighbors disagree about a sighting, the design keeps both notes and labels the disagreement, because a log that hides disagreement loses credibility.

title: Signature Evidence Vault
body:
Overview

The Signature Evidence Vault is a Signature forensic preservation design for drone sighting evidence: original files, hash notes, and a chain-of-custody log kept in plain order. It treats a photograph or log as evidence only while its original is untouched, so the design protects originals and works from copies. Its lawful use is a property owner, event team, or school keeping sighting evidence in a form an authority can trust. A vault cannot authenticate a photograph's content, cannot prove what a camera saw, and cannot replace an authority's own investigation.

How the Signature design works

The vault has three drawers. The first drawer holds originals: photographs, videos, and log exports, copied once from the capturing device and then never opened for editing. The second drawer holds a hash note for each original: a short fingerprint computed from the file, so that any later change to the file would change the fingerprint. The third drawer holds the custody log: who captured the file, when it was copied, who holds it now, and to whom it was sent, each entry dated. Working copies for viewing, cropping for a report, or sharing with staff come from the originals but never replace them, and the custody log records every copy sent out.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can use the vault to hand an authority an original photograph with a matching hash note, rather than a forwarded copy of a copy. An event team can use it to keep a day's log exports intact for a later question. A school can use it to show that a sighting note was written the same day and never altered. The lawful value is trust: an authority that receives an intact original with a custody note can rely on it more fully than on a loose attachment.

Limits

Hash notes prove that a file is unchanged since the note was made; they do not prove that the file shows what its caption claims, and they do not prove the time a camera's clock claimed. A vault also cannot protect evidence that was never captured, and it cannot recover a deleted original. The design is honest about this: preservation protects what exists, and it must never be presented as proof of the facts inside the file.

Signature original

files = ['sighting-1804.jpg', 'log-2026-10-25.txt']
for f in files:
    h = hashlib.sha256(f.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
    print(f + ': vault fingerprint ' + h + ' (original untouched)')
print('Evidence Vault: 2 originals preserved, custody log entries: 2')

title: Signature Claim Ledger
body:
Overview

The Signature Claim Ledger is a Signature insurance and liability ledger design for drone-related incidents affecting civilians: what happened, what it cost, and what was reported, in one tidy book. It is a private record book, not a legal judgment: it organizes facts for an insurer, a property owner, or an authority, without deciding fault. Its lawful use is a homeowner or small business keeping incident facts and costs in order after a genuine incident, such as property damage or a disrupted event. A ledger cannot decide liability, cannot value a claim by itself, and cannot substitute for an insurer's process or a legal proceeding.

How the Signature design works

Each ledger entry has five fields: date and time, place, factual description, evidence reference, and cost note. The factual description sticks to what was seen and what was damaged, in plain words, without attributing motive or naming a suspected operator. The evidence reference points to the Evidence Vault entry for the same incident, so that photographs and logs sit beside the ledger rather than inside it. The cost note records repair quotes, receipts, or event costs in the owner's own figures, labeled as the owner's figures rather than as settled amounts. A running total sums the cost notes, and each entry carries a status: noted, reported, or resolved, so that the book shows at a glance what still needs attention.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner whose garden structure was damaged can use the ledger to give an insurer one ordered account instead of scattered notes. A small venue whose event was disrupted can use it to record lost costs factually for a later discussion. The lawful value is order: a clean book helps insurers, owners, and authorities reach the facts quickly, and it prevents a genuine incident from being lost in a drawer of loose papers.

Limits

The ledger records the owner's account; it does not prove causation, does not establish that any particular aircraft caused the damage, and does not set a value an insurer must accept. Where facts are disputed, the ledger keeps the dispute visible rather than resolving it. Owners with a real claim should follow their insurer's process and seek local advice where needed, because a tidy book supports a claim but never replaces the process that decides it.

title: Signature Defense Catalog
body:
Overview

The Signature Defense Catalog is a Signature product-class catalog for civilian-legal classes only: detection, sensing, barriers, and documentation tools described by class, not by vendor. It organizes the civilian field so that a newcomer can see the classes, compare their purposes, and choose a lawful starting point. Its lawful use is education and planning: a property owner or organizer reading class descriptions before deciding what, if anything, to adopt. The catalog lists classes, never vendors or models, and it excludes any class meant to interfere with aircraft or to serve a military purpose.

How the Signature design works

The catalog has four shelves. Detection holds sound listeners, sky cameras, and broadcast readers, each described by what it senses and what it logs. Sensing holds radar and spectrum survey classes, described by range class and by what they cannot identify. Barriers holds passive property classes, such as garden netting and window coverings, described as property features with their own planning notes. Documentation holds logs, chains, vaults, and ledgers, described as the paper and file practices that turn a sighting into a usable report. Each class entry carries a purpose line, a lawful-use line, and a limits line, in the same order, so that classes can be compared fairly.

Lawful civilian use

A homeowner can read the catalog's four shelves and decide that documentation alone suits their needs, without buying anything. An event organizer can read it and choose detection plus documentation for a large outdoor show. A school can read it and choose procedure plus documentation, which costs nothing but attention. The lawful value is orientation: a newcomer sees the whole civilian field at a glance and can ask better questions of any supplier, authority, or adviser.

Limits

A catalog of classes cannot recommend a product, cannot verify a supplier's claims, and cannot keep pace with every new device; classes are stable, products change quickly. The catalog also cannot grant legality: a class described here may still be restricted in a particular place or use, and local rules govern. Readers must check published rules before adopting any class, and must treat every class entry's limits line as part of the entry, not as fine print.

title: Signature Home Defense Plan
body:
Overview

The Signature Home Defense Plan is a Signature end-to-end home plan that ties every earlier design into one household document: watch, document, report, and preserve, in that order. It is the capstone of this database: a single plan a household can print, brief, and rehearse, covering ordinary days and unusual evenings alike. Its lawful use is a household agreeing in advance on roles, tools, and reporting steps, so that a real sighting meets a plan rather than improvisation. A plan cannot control the sky, cannot authorize action against any aircraft, and cannot promise that any sighting will be resolved.

How the Signature design works

The plan has five pages. Page one names the household roles: watcher, writer, and caller, with backups for each. Page two lists the household's chosen tools from this database, such as a sound listener, a sky camera, or simply a notebook, with where each tool sits and who checks it. Page three draws the property zones: garden, patio, and street-facing areas, with the fence-keeper polygons noted. Page four writes the response ladder and the alert chain for the household, including the contact for the property owner and the local authority. Page five covers preservation and the claim ledger: where originals are kept, who holds the vault, and how costs are noted. The plan ends with a rehearsal date, because a plan no one has practiced is a hope, not a plan.

Lawful civilian use

A family can adopt the plan in one evening meeting, assign roles to adults, and brief older children on the single rule that matters: tell an adult, do not chase or confront. A household with a home business can adapt the plan to cover clients and deliveries. The lawful product is a calm, practiced household that documents well and reports well, which is the full extent of what a civilian household should aim to do.

Limits

The plan's limits are the database's limits, stated once more at the end so that no reader misses them: observation and documentation are the household's tools, enforcement belongs to authorities, and interference with any aircraft is outside the plan entirely. The plan cannot adapt itself: it must be reviewed when the household moves, when tools change, or when local rules change, and a stale plan is treated as suspect until reviewed. A household that keeps its plan current, its roles assigned, and its notes factual has done the job this database sets out.
